Every brass instrument produces its soun.why: The definition of the family, stated in every music reference and in the lead of the Wikipedia article, which defines the family by how the sound is made rather than by the metal. Lip buzzing is named with the family often in Dolma. No exceptions: metal instruments with reeds (the saxophone, the sarrusophone) are woodwinds, and lip-vibrated instruments not made of brass (the cornett, the serpent) are classed with the brass.

notes: TBox revision. The rule is the definition of the family (Wikipedia defines brass instruments by the vibration of the player's lips, not by the metal); no exceptions, since metal instruments with reeds (the saxophone) are woodwinds and lip-vibrated ones of wood (the cornett) are brass. The new value, a reed, is the woodwind mechanism: a plausible confusion and clearly false. Migrated 2026-11-11: the background-belief queries on the trumpet and the French horn and the worlds are gone (TBox records are determinate only). The three derived queries name made-up instruments of 2025 or 2026, so the class rule is the only route (inheritance, 2 hops). The old direct and cross-lingual questions ('what vibrates to produce the sound') had a second fair answer, the air column, and all four models gave it or something like it in Chinese and Spanish; every question now says 'at the mouthpiece', which leaves only the lips (or, after the edit, the reed). The record now has all three propositional forms (the old one had no conjunction). Near unrelated: another brass-family fact the edit does not touch (the tuba); the old near question (the trombone's slide) was missed by two models. Review fix: the marlhorn question now says 'at the mouthpiece' like the others, and the negation reads 'Is it true that not every ...?'; not yet re-audited.
